clinicalPearls: Caused by cystinuria, an autosomal recessive defect of dibasic amino-acid transport in the proximal tubule due to mutations in SLC3A1 or SLC7A9
Impaired reabsorption of cystine, together with ornithine, lysine and arginine, leaves poorly soluble cystine to precipitate in the urine
Classically presents in childhood or early adulthood with recurrent stones and a strong family history
Pathognomonic flat hexagonal cystine crystals may be seen on microscopy of acidic, concentrated urine
Stones are only faintly radio-opaque, giving a ground-glass appearance, and are easily overlooked on plain films because of their sulphur content
A positive urinary cyanide-nitroprusside test screens for excess cystine excretion
Management aims to keep cystine soluble through a high fluid intake spread across day and night, urinary alkalinisation with potassium citrate, and moderation of dietary sodium and animal protein
Thiol (cystine-binding) agents such as tiopronin or penicillamine are added when conservative measures fail to control stone formation
reference.pathophysiology: Cystinuria results from biallelic mutations in the genes encoding the two subunits of the proximal tubular transporter for cystine and the dibasic amino acids, SLC3A1 (encoding rBAT) and SLC7A9 (encoding b0,+AT). Defective reabsorption leaves large amounts of cystine in the tubular fluid; because cystine is relatively insoluble, especially in acidic and concentrated urine, it becomes supersaturated and crystallises. Solubility improves markedly as the urine is diluted and alkalinised, which underpins the therapeutic approach. The disorder generates recurrent stones from early life and, without control, a substantial cumulative stone burden.
additionalDifferentials: Other rare metabolic stones such as xanthine or 2,8-dihydroxyadenine
additionalInvestigations: Urine microscopy for the pathognomonic hexagonal cystine crystals
Non-contrast CT to assess stone burden, since plain films underestimate it
Genetic testing for SLC3A1 or SLC7A9 in selected cases and screening of family members
redFlags: Recurrent obstruction with progressive renal impairment from repeated stone episodes
A very high stone burden in childhood threatening long-term renal function
reference.prognosis: A lifelong condition with a strong tendency to recur; with rigorous hydration, alkalinisation and thiol therapy the stone rate can be greatly reduced, but adherence is demanding and chronic kidney disease may develop after repeated interventions.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis in a young recurrent stone-former with a family history
Relying on plain radiographs, which poorly demonstrate faintly opaque cystine stones
Under-prescribing hydration, particularly overnight when the urine concentrates
Delaying thiol therapy until extensive renal damage has already occurred
management: Maintain high fluid intake throughout day and night to dilute the urine and keep cystine below its saturation point
Alkalinise the urine with potassium citrate, as cystine solubility improves markedly at higher urinary pH
Restrict dietary sodium and moderate animal protein to lower urinary cystine excretion
Add thiol-based cystine-binding agents such as tiopronin or penicillamine for high excretors or disease refractory to hydration and alkalinisation
Remove obstructing or large stones with ureteroscopic laser lithotripsy or percutaneous nephrolithotomy, as cystine stones resist extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy
Monitor with periodic 24-hour urinary cystine, urine pH and imaging surveillance of stone burden to preserve renal function
Provide genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder and screen family members
